summary: Describes the correct procedure for incrementally updating the Internet checksum when only part of a packet changes, so it need not be recomputed from scratch. It replaces the description in RFC 1071. It is an implementation technique, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains how to adjust an IP checksum when a packet field changes, rather than calculating the checksum from scratch. It clarifies that the calculation uses the complemented value stored in the packet and one's-complement arithmetic.

subtitle: Shows how to update an Internet checksum after changing a packet field.

tldr.problem: Recomputing an entire IP checksum is unnecessary when only one field changes, but the earlier update equation was difficult to apply directly to the stored checksum.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives an update rule for the complement stored in the checksum field, using one's-complement arithmetic, and illustrates it with TTL changes.
tldr.outcome: This is an implementation technique, not a standard. It is updated by RFC 1624, according to the unit metadata.

today: RFC 1141 is listed as Informational and is updated by RFC 1624, according to the unit metadata. It was intended to replace the incremental-update description in RFC 1071.

sections.title: Why an Incremental Rule Helps
sections.content:
RFC 1071 describes updating an IP checksum when a field changes, instead of recomputing the entire checksum. This memo says the earlier equation updates the checksum value itself, while the packet stores its one's complement.

The earlier notation also did not make clear that all arithmetic, including negation, uses one's-complement arithmetic. The memo restates the calculation in a form that can be applied to the stored field.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet stores the complement of the checksum, so an update rule needs to work with that stored value. This memo also makes clear which arithmetic to use.

sections.title: Updating the Stored Checksum
sections.content:
The memo gives the update rule as ~C' = ~C + m + ~m', using one's-complement addition. Here, the old and new values of the changed field adjust the complemented checksum value.

For the common case where an IP TTL decreases by one, the checksum field is adjusted by adding 1 or 256, as appropriate, with one's-complement addition.
sections.plainLanguage: Adjust the stored checksum using the old and new field values, with one's-complement addition. For a one-step TTL decrease, the memo says to add 1 or 256 as appropriate.

sections.title: TTL Code Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows one non-portable big-endian C example for decreasing the TTL by one and adding 0x100 to the checksum. It also gives a more general routine that decreases the TTL by a chosen amount and folds carries back into the result.

The memo says the special case can be optimized in different ways and notes that compiler behavior may vary.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples update a checksum when the TTL changes. One handles a decrease by one, and another handles a specified decrease.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that it does not address security issues. It describes only a calculation for updating an existing Internet checksum after a field changes.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains checksum arithmetic only. It does not discuss security issues.
